in S. Place and walked slowly, as though in

notes.english: a tiny room at the very top of the house. attic, basically.
notes.simple: the small room right under the roof.
notes.aloud: a garret, the small room under the roof, where the rent is cheapest.

notes.english: lived there as a renter, a room, not a home.
notes.simple: he rented the room. it was never his.
notes.aloud: lodged. He paid rent on one room, and that was the whole of it.

notes.english: pausing because you can't decide. his whole personality, honestly.
notes.aloud: hesitation, stopping because you cannot decide. that is the man, and the book.

notes.english: old English for 'yourself.' Marcus is talking to himself, the whole book is a private diary.
notes.simple: an old word for 'yourself.' he is writing to himself.
notes.aloud: thyself, the old word for yourself. Marcus is talking to Marcus; the book is his diary.

notes.english: someone far too interested in everyone else's business.
notes.simple: someone too interested in other people's business.
notes.aloud: a busy-body, the one who is far too interested in everybody else's business.

notes.english: cold to other people, the opposite of a good neighbour. Rome had them too.
notes.simple: cold with other people. a bad neighbour.
notes.aloud: unsocial, cold with everyone, the opposite of a good neighbour. Rome had them too.

companions.title: Crime and Punishment
companions.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
companions.opening: Six parts and an epilogue, and the crime is over early. This book is about everything after. Tell me where your bookmark sits and we'll talk about the rest.
themes: Whether a person can be extraordinary enough to step over the rules, and what the stepping over costs.
Guilt as a physical illness: fever, fainting, the body confessing before the mouth does.
Petersburg itself (heat, crowds, closet-sized rooms) pressing on every decision.
Poverty and what it makes people rationalize, from pawnshops to marriages.
Confession as a need rather than a defeat, the pull toward being known.

characters.name: Rodion Raskolnikov
characters.note: A former student in a garret with a theory he hasn't said out loud yet.

characters.name: Alyona Ivanovna
characters.note: The pawnbroker on the fourth floor, sharp on interest, short on sympathy.

characters.name: Semyon Marmeladov
characters.note: A ruined clerk who narrates his own downfall in a tavern, in detail, to a stranger.

characters.name: Dmitri Razumikhin
characters.note: The friend Raskolnikov doesn't deserve, practical, loud, permanently broke and permanently cheerful.

characters.name: Sonya Marmeladova
characters.note: Marmeladov's daughter, who carries the family and says little; she matters more with every part.

characters.name: Dunya
characters.note: Raskolnikov's sister, engaged for practical reasons her brother refuses to accept.

characters.name: Porfiry Petrovich
characters.note: The examining magistrate. Friendly, digressive, and never once off duty.

characters.name: Svidrigailov
characters.note: Dunya's former employer, arrived in Petersburg with money and unfinished intentions.

beats.note: The theory has left the garret: the old pawnbroker and her sister Lizaveta are dead, and Raskolnikov is home with what he took, having proved nothing he hoped to.

The loot sits untouched under a stone. Raskolnikov has cycled through fever, a police summons that turned out to be about rent, and a near-confession over tea in a café. Marmeladov is dead in the street, Sonya has a face now, and his mother and sister have arrived at the worst possible moment.

Luzhin has been measured and found small. Porfiry has held his first interview (pleasant, circular, terrifying) with Raskolnikov's own article on extraordinary men now in the room. A stranger on the street has said the word 'murderer,' and someone new is standing in the doorway.

The doorway man was Svidrigailov, making offers nobody asked for. Luzhin has been shown out of the family. Sonya has read the raising of Lazarus aloud to the one man in Petersburg who asked for it, and at the second interview a painter named Mikolka confessed to the murder, which should be a relief, and isn't.

Luzhin's revenge, a hundred-rouble note planted on Sonya, collapsed in public. Katerina Ivanovna has died in the street, mad and unbowed. And Raskolnikov has told Sonya the thing itself; her answer was the crossroads: bow, kiss the earth, confess. He hasn't. Yet.

Porfiry said it plainly, no games, you did it, confession buys a discount. Svidrigailov let Dunya walk out with the revolver still warm, settled his accounts, and took what he called his trip to America. Raskolnikov kissed the earth at the Haymarket and said the words at the station.
Siberia. Eight years, second class; Sonya followed the convoy. The epilogue's whole argument is one plague-dream and one morning by the river, whether a theory can die and the man survive it.

companions.spoilerLine: That's on a later page than yours. Confessions arrive in their own time, read on and ask me again.

companions.title: Meditations
companions.author: Marcus Aurelius
companions.opening: Twelve books of a private notebook that was never meant to leave the tent. There's no plot to spoil, only an argument that keeps returning, tell me which book you're in.
themes: You will die, and the point of remembering it is scheduling: do the thing in front of you.
The inner citadel, the one territory no emperor or annoyance can occupy without your consent.
Other people are difficult by nature, and dealing with them kindly is the actual exercise.
Nature as one organism: what happens to you is weather, not persecution.
The strangeness of reading advice a man wrote strictly to himself.

characters.name: Marcus Aurelius
characters.note: The author and the sole intended reader. Emperor of Rome, writing at night, in Greek.

characters.name: Antoninus Pius
characters.note: His adoptive father, thanked at length in Book 1 as the model of holding power quietly.

characters.name: Rusticus
characters.note: The teacher who told him to stop performing rhetoric and lent him Epictetus. Book 1 credits him with the whole project.

characters.name: Epictetus
characters.note: A former slave whose lectures echo through the notebook, the philosophy's other voice.

characters.name: Heraclitus
characters.note: The old philosopher of flux, cited when Marcus wants reminding that even philosophers die of ordinary things.

beats.note: Book 1 is the ledger of debts: everything Marcus believes, credited line by line to the person he learned it from, family, teachers, the gods, in that order.

The practice has begun in earnest: mornings open by expecting difficult people, death is treated as a deadline rather than a tragedy, and the notebook keeps circling one instruction, attend to the task in front of you.

The frame has widened to the whole cosmos: one nature, one substance, everything recycled. Do good and expect no witness; fame turns out to be spectacularly bad arithmetic once you set it against time.

The middle books grind at the hardest material (injury, anger, other people's failings) and keep reaching the same verdict: the wrong belongs to the one doing it, and your retreat is always available, being internal.

The closing books make peace with the exit: death is nature's business, handled competently for everyone so far. The last entry says to leave the stage gracefully, the one dismissing you is the one who hired you.

companions.spoilerLine: Strictly speaking a diary can't be spoiled, but the argument earns its later entries. Read to that book and ask me again.

companions.title: The Little Prince
companions.author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
companions.opening: Twenty-seven short chapters, a desert, and a visitor who asks questions instead of answering them. Tell me which chapter you've reached and we'll talk, no further.
themes: Grown-ups: how counting, owning, and being sensible slowly replace seeing.
Taming, the idea that time spent on someone is what makes them matter.
Small responsibilities kept faithfully: one flower, three volcanoes, a daily sweep for baobabs.
What's essential being invisible to the eye, and what it costs to learn that.
Loneliness, and the difference between being alone and being untamed.

characters.name: The narrator
characters.note: A pilot whose drawing career ended at age six, reviewed badly by adults.

characters.name: The little prince
characters.note: Arrives in the Sahara asking for a sheep. Declines to answer questions; never lets go of one he's asked.

characters.name: The rose
characters.note: Vain, four thorns, dearly loved. The reason for everything, including the leaving.

characters.name: The king
characters.note: First stop on the tour of grown-ups: rules an empty planet, only issues orders that would be obeyed anyway.

characters.name: The snake
characters.note: The first meeting on Earth. Speaks in riddles and offers a favor best considered carefully.

characters.name: The fox
characters.note: Asks to be tamed and explains how. Owns the book's secret and gives it away at parting.

beats.note: A pilot is down in the Sahara with eight days of water, and a small visitor has appeared asking for a sheep. The drawings have resumed after a long retirement, and the visitor turns out to come from an asteroid about the size of a house.

The prince's planet stands fully surveyed: three knee-high volcanoes, baobab weeding, forty-odd sunsets on a sad day, and a rose who is proud, demanding, and loved. Her games ended in his leaving; she managed not to cry in front of him, barely.

Six planets, six grown-ups: a king with no subjects, an admirer with no audience, a drinker drinking to forget the drinking, a businessman counting stars he owns, a lamplighter obeying an absurd order faithfully, and a geographer who never leaves the desk. Only the lamplighter escaped ridicule. He attends to something besides himself.

Earth at last, entered through the empty desert: a snake who talks in riddles, a mountain that only echoes, and then a garden of five thousand roses, hard news for a prince who believed his was the only one in the universe.

The fox has been tamed and has said the thing plainly: what's essential is invisible to the eye, and the time spent on your rose is what makes her matter. Back in the desert the narrator's water has run out, a night of walking, and at daybreak, a well.

The well gave up its water at dawn. The rest you've read: the anniversary of the arrival, the arrangement with the snake, the fall no louder than sand, and a narrator who still checks the night sky and asks you to do the same.

companions.spoilerLine: That happens past your bookmark, and nothing essential is visible from here, read on and ask again.

companions.title: The Brothers Karamazov
companions.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
companions.opening: Twelve books, three brothers, and one father too many. Tell me which book you're in and we'll keep the conversation on the near side of it.
themes: Whether anything is permitted if God isn't watching, the family runs the experiment live.
Fathers and sons: inheritance as grievance, biology as accusation.
Faith that survives doubt versus doubt that can't survive itself.
Active love as a discipline, harsh and dreadful next to love in dreams.
Responsibility for all: the claim that everyone is guilty before everyone, taken literally.

characters.name: Fyodor Pavlovich Karamazov
characters.note: The father. A buffoon by strategy, a sensualist by conviction, a landowner by accident.

characters.name: Dmitri (Mitya)
characters.note: The eldest brother: an officer's temper and an inheritance grievance he considers a moral cause.

characters.name: Ivan
characters.note: The middle brother, the educated one, published, polite, and quietly on fire.

characters.name: Alyosha
characters.note: The youngest, a novice at the local monastery; the narrator's favorite and everyone's messenger.

characters.name: Elder Zosima
characters.note: Alyosha's elder at the monastery, dying, beloved, and about to referee a family that can't be refereed.

characters.name: Smerdyakov
characters.note: The cook. Epileptic, exact, offended by everything, and listening more than anyone notices.

characters.name: Grushenka
characters.note: The woman both father and eldest son circle, the local legend precedes her; the person turns out to be someone else.

characters.name: Katerina Ivanovna
characters.note: Dmitri's betrothed, magnificent, wounded, and generous in ways that cost the recipient.

beats.note: The family is assembled and already at war: the Karamazov history behind us, and a peace meeting in the elder's cell that the father turned into theater. It ended with the elder bowing to the ground before Dmitri, and nobody, including the monastery, agrees on what that meant.

The sensualists in full: father and eldest son open rivals for Grushenka, with the inheritance as pretext. Smerdyakov's whole story is on the table now (his mother, his epilepsy, his opinions) Dmitri has made his 'confession of an ardent heart' to Alyosha, and the father has been dragged by the beard in his own house.

The lacerations: Katerina's two hundred roubles sent to Captain Snegiryov (the man Dmitri dragged from the tavern by the beard, in front of his boy Ilyusha) and refused with a stamp of the heel. Pride, it turns out, is the one thing in this town nobody can afford and everybody buys.

Ivan has laid his cards down: the catalogue of tortured children, the ticket respectfully returned, and the Grand Inquisitor, a poem about a church that corrected God's work. And in a courtyard chat with Smerdyakov, things were said with plausible deniability that will not stay deniable.

Book 6 gave the answer as a life rather than an argument (Zosima's brother Markel, the duel, everyone guilty before everyone. Then the elder died, and his body did the one thing the town demanded it not do: decayed on schedule. Alyosha's faith cracked on the smell of it, spent an evening at Grushenka's, and came back changed) the chapter called Cana of Galilee is where the book lets him weep and stand up.

The night everything happened: Dmitri hunting three thousand roubles across the district, a brass pestle in his pocket, the garden fence, old Grigory struck down, and a spree at Mokroye interrupted by officials at dawn. Fyodor Pavlovich is dead; Dmitri, covered in exactly the wrong evidence, is under arrest and swearing to the one gap in his story.

Three visits to Smerdyakov, and on the last one Ivan got the full accounting, who did what, and on whose theory. The same night the devil paid Ivan a personal call, shabby suit and all, and Smerdyakov closed his own account with a rope. The trial opens with the only confession that matters unavailable.

The trial in full: the evidence marching one way, Ivan breaking down mid-testimony, Katerina's letter detonating, and twelve peasants who, as the town put it, stood up for themselves. A miscarriage, formally. Then the epilogue at the stone, where Alyosha and the boys agree to remember one good thing each; the book ends on a cheer.

companions.spoilerLine: That sits in a later book than yours. Everyone in this family answers eventually, read on and ask me again.

companions.author: George Orwell
companions.opening: Three parts, and each one changes what kind of book you think you're reading. Tell me where you are; I'll keep the rest behind the telescreen.
themes: Language as a cage: if the word for a thought is gone, is the thought?
Surveillance that works less by watching than by making you assume it is.
The past as an editable document, and memory as the last private property.
Whether love between two people can count as a political act.
The proles, the eighty-five percent the Party barely bothers to watch, and why.

characters.name: Winston Smith
characters.note: Thirty-nine, varicose ulcer, rewrites old newspapers for a living, and has started noticing that he does.

characters.name: Julia
characters.note: The dark-haired girl from the Fiction Department. Winston has decided he hates her, on no particular evidence.

characters.name: O'Brien
characters.note: Inner Party. Winston reads sympathy into one glance from him, which is either hope or the start of a mistake.

characters.name: Mr Charrington
characters.note: The old man who keeps the junk shop where Winston bought his diary. Fond of the past, helpfully.

characters.name: Syme
characters.note: A Newspeak lexicographer, brilliant and doomed by his own clear sight. Winston can see it, and so can Syme, almost.

characters.name: Parsons
characters.note: Winston's neighbor: sweaty, loyal, proud of children who inform on people.

beats.note: A diary has been opened, which is not illegal because nothing is, merely fatal. Winston has committed thoughtcrime in ink, filed the dark-haired girl under enemy and O'Brien under maybe, and started buying nostalgia at Mr Charrington's shop. DOWN WITH BIG BROTHER, says the page, repeatedly.

The note said what it said, and the affair now has a geography: a clearing in the country, a church belfry, and the room over the junk shop with no telescreen in it. 'We are the dead' has become pillow talk, which both of them believe and neither acts like.

O'Brien made contact. The visit to his flat came with wine, a catechism of what they'd be willing to do, and the promise of Goldstein's book, which Winston was reading aloud in the room over the shop, right up until the voice behind the picture finished the thought.

The Ministry of Love, where it was always going to end: the cell with no darkness, O'Brien on the wrong side of the table (or, as he'd insist, the right one) the sessions, Room 101, and the chestnut tree café after. Two plus two, the gin, and the last line about love.
One more thing: the appendix on Newspeak is written in the past tense, in standard English. Nobody at the Ministry approved that. Worth sitting with.

companions.spoilerLine: That's past your bookmark, and I don't give away what's ahead of it. Read on and ask again.

companions.title: Notes from Underground
companions.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
companions.opening: Two parts: first the argument, then the incident that proves it. Forty pages of a man talking to himself, then the week he'd rather forget. Tell me which part you're in.
themes: Spite as a form of freedom, choosing badly just to prove the choosing is yours.
Consciousness as an illness: seeing every side of everything until action is impossible.
The crystal palace, utopias, and the human need to kick them.
Two times two is four, and the part of us that resents it.
Humiliation as a habit that starts to look like a personality.

characters.name: The Underground Man
characters.note: Forty, retired from a civil service job he hated, narrating from a corner he calls the underground. Warns you on page one that he is sick, spiteful, and lying.

characters.name: The officer
characters.note: A soldier who once moved him aside like furniture, inspiring a revenge plot measured in years and one overcoat collar.

characters.name: Simonov
characters.note: The old schoolmate who still, reluctantly, answers the door, banker of the dinner and of small loans.

characters.name: Zverkov
characters.note: Another schoolmate: successful, generous, pleasant, which is unforgivable. Guest of honor at a farewell dinner our narrator invites himself to.

characters.name: Liza
characters.note: Twenty, new to the establishment on the night the narrator arrives with a speech loaded. She listens, which he did not plan for.

characters.name: Apollon
characters.note: The narrator's servant, dignified beyond his wages, waging a cold war of pauses.

beats.note: The confession is underway: a sick, spiteful, unattractive man (his words, in that order) explaining why he never became anything, and why the fault lies with consciousness itself. Even his toothache, he admits, gets performed.

The argument has found its target: the crystal palace, the calculated utopia where every choice is arithmetic. His objection stands, a man will go mad on purpose rather than be a piano key. Two times two is four, he concedes; but two times two is five is sometimes very charming.

The evidence, apropos of the wet snow: years spent engineering one shoulder-bump against an officer who never noticed him, then the Zverkov dinner (uninvited, under-dressed, pacing the room for three hours while they ignored him) ending with him trailing the party to the establishment they'd moved on to.

Liza happened. The grand speech about her future worked better than he intended, so he left his address and spent days dreading the knock. She came, caught him mid-tantrum in all his poverty, and understood him anyway, for which he pressed a five-rouble note into her hand. She left it crumpled on the table and walked into the snow, and he didn't catch her. He'd like you to know he's ashamed of the whole account, and that this proves his point.

companions.spoilerLine: That's ahead of your page. He'd spite me for telling it early, read on and ask again.

companions.title: White Nights
companions.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
companions.opening: Four nights on a Petersburg embankment and one morning after. It's short and it's tender, and I won't hurry it, which night are you on?
themes: The dreamer's life: fifteen years of imagined friendships and one real conversation.
Petersburg's white nights, when the sky won't darken and nobody quite goes home.
Loneliness so practiced it has furniture, and what happens when someone sits down in it.
Gratitude as a form of love, and whether it's enough.
Whether one perfect minute can fund a whole life.

characters.name: The dreamer
characters.note: Unnamed, twenty-six, knows every building in Petersburg by sight and no people at all. Our narrator.

characters.name: Nastenka
characters.note: Seventeen, met crying at a canal railing. Sets one condition on the friendship: don't fall in love with her.

characters.name: The grandmother
characters.note: Blind, formidable, and in the habit of pinning Nastenka's dress to her own so the girl can't wander.

characters.name: The lodger
characters.note: The boarder from the grandmother's house in Nastenka's story, took the two women to the opera, then left for Moscow with a promise attached.

characters.name: Matryona
characters.note: The dreamer's housekeeper, at war with the cobwebs and losing on schedule.

beats.note: One meeting so far: a girl crying at the canal railing, an unpleasant gentleman seen off, and an agreement struck. She'll be there tomorrow, and he is not to fall in love. He has accepted the terms in the way people accept terms.

Histories exchanged. His: fifteen years of dreaming instead of living, confessed with alarming fluency. Hers: a blind grandmother, a pin, and a lodger who promised to come back within the year. The year is up, he's known to be in Petersburg, and no word has come, so the dreamer has offered to carry a letter.

The letter is delivered, and the third night was spent waiting for a man who didn't come. Nastenka ran the whole scale from hope to despair; the dreamer held his own news back, namely that the condition she set on the first night has already been broken, on his side.

No letter, no lodger, and the dreamer finally said it. Nastenka, weeping, resolved to love him instead, lodgings discussed, a future sketched right there on the embankment. Then a young man passed under the lamp, and she went very still.

Morning, and her letter came: gratitude, apology, a wedding, and a request for the cruelest thing, friendship. The dreamer's answer is the famous last line, a blessing where a grievance would fit: a whole minute of bliss, and enough for a lifetime.

companions.spoilerLine: That's a later night than yours. The embankment keeps its own schedule, read on and ask me again.

companions.title: The Idiot
companions.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
companions.opening: Four parts, beginning on a third-class train into Petersburg with two men who should never have met. Tell me which part you're in, and we'll stop the conversation at that station.
themes: What happens to a genuinely good person in a society that has priced everything.
Beauty, whether it saves the world or gets people killed; the book keeps both options open.
Money as weather: dowries, inheritances, and bundles of banknotes altering every room they enter.
Illness and insight, the still, clear second before the fall.
Compassion versus passion, aimed at the same woman, with no stable middle.

characters.name: Prince Myshkin
characters.note: Last of his line, back from a Swiss sanatorium with a small bundle, an epilepsy diagnosis, and no idea what things cost.

characters.name: Rogozhin
characters.note: Met on the train: a merchant's son, a new inheritance, and one fixed idea with a woman's name on it.

characters.name: Lebedev
characters.note: Also on the train, agreeing with everyone. A clerk who knows everything about everybody and lends it out at interest.

characters.name: Nastasya Filippovna
characters.note: First a photograph, then a legend, then a person, kept since girlhood by the man who ruined her, and pricing herself accordingly.

characters.name: Ganya
characters.note: The Epanchins' secretary, handsome and mediocre, trying to marry his way out of both conditions.

characters.name: Aglaya
characters.note: The youngest Epanchin daughter: the beauty of the family, bored, sharp, and waiting for something worth the sharpness.

characters.name: Ippolit
characters.note: Seventeen and dying of consumption, determined that somebody acknowledge it meaningfully.

beats.note: One Petersburg day, start to finish: the train, the Epanchins disarmed by plain frankness, the story of the execution, the photograph, and the birthday party where Nastasya Filippovna put a hundred thousand roubles into the fire, told Ganya it was his if he'd reach in barehanded, watched him faint instead, and drove off into the night with Rogozhin.

Six months of Moscow, skipped and rumored, and the prince is back. The visit to Rogozhin's dark house brought an exchange of crosses under a copy of Holbein's dead Christ, brotherhood declared, with a garden knife that kept being on the table anyway. On a hotel staircase the knife finally came out; the epileptic fit arrived first, and nobody has to say what it prevented.

Pavlovsk in season: verandas, scandal sheets, and Ippolit's 'Necessary Explanation' read aloud at dawn with a suicide planned as punctuation, the pistol misfired, and the mortification did not. Meanwhile the green bench: Aglaya and the prince are being talked about because there is something to talk about, and Nastasya has begun writing Aglaya letters, which is nobody's idea of good news.

Everything at once: the engagement party where the prince talked too long and broke the Chinese vase exactly as prophesied; the meeting of the two women that could only end one way and did; the wedding Nastasya fled at the church door, with Rogozhin; and the vigil in the dark house on Gorokhovaya, two men side by side over what's behind the curtain, and the prince gone back to where the book found him, only further.

companions.spoilerLine: That's past your part, and this ending should not arrive early, read on and ask me again.

recommendations.title: White Nights
recommendations.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
recommendations.why: Proof the man behind Crime and Punishment could be gentle, four nights on an embankment, one morning after.

recommendations.title: Crime and Punishment
recommendations.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
recommendations.why: You've been circling Dostoevsky. This is the door most readers enter by, and it holds.

recommendations.title: The Idiot
recommendations.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
recommendations.why: His experiment after Crime and Punishment: swap the murderer for a genuinely good man, and watch Petersburg handle him no more kindly.

recommendations.title: Demons
recommendations.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
recommendations.why: You shelved 1984. Dostoevsky watched the same machinery being assembled a half-century early, in a provincial town, over tea.

recommendations.title: The Gambler
recommendations.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
recommendations.why: You know Dostoevsky's fevers by now. This one he wrote in twenty-six days to pay his own roulette debts, so the research was primary.

recommendations.title: Humiliated and Insulted
recommendations.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
recommendations.why: You shelved Poor Folk. This is that early tenderness come back from Siberia with harder edges and a bigger cast.

recommendations.title: The Double
recommendations.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
recommendations.why: You shelved The Trial. Kafka's nightmare logic starts here, with a Petersburg clerk whose exact copy turns out to be better at his life.

recommendations.title: The Trial
recommendations.author: Franz Kafka
recommendations.why: You shelved The Double, the same nightmare a lifetime later: Golyadkin lost his self, Josef K. loses his case, and neither is told why.

recommendations.author: George Orwell
recommendations.why: You shelved The Trial. Orwell gives Kafka's nameless court a ministry, a language, and a filing system.

recommendations.title: The Stranger
recommendations.author: Albert Camus
recommendations.why: You shelved Notes from Underground. Meursault is the opposite failure: where the Underground Man explains too much, he won't explain at all, and the court notices.

recommendations.title: Meditations
recommendations.author: Marcus Aurelius
recommendations.why: You shelved Atomic Habits. This is the original habit journal, kept nightly by a Roman emperor with no intention of publishing.

recommendations.title: Sapiens
recommendations.author: Yuval Noah Harari
recommendations.why: You shelved Meditations. Marcus takes the long view of one life; Harari takes it of the whole species.

recommendations.title: The Little Prince
recommendations.author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
recommendations.why: You shelved White Nights, the other tender one in the catalog: a downed pilot, a visiting prince, and a rose worth the trouble.

recommendations.title: Atomic Habits
recommendations.author: James Clear
recommendations.why: You shelved Deep Work. Newport clears the desk, Clear is the one who gets you back to it every morning.

recommendations.title: Deep Work
recommendations.author: Cal Newport
recommendations.why: You shelved Clean Code, the code gets cleaner when the attention does; this is the working case for a shut door.

recommendations.title: A Brief History of Time
recommendations.author: Stephen Hawking
recommendations.why: You shelved Sapiens. If seventy thousand years felt brief, Hawking offers thirteen billion and change.
